passage:
"Akash, did you read what you sent the club group?" Bhavna held up her phone.
"The trek message? Yeah. Clear, right?"
"It's ALL IN CAPITALS. 'EVERYONE MUST BRING SHOES. NO EXCUSES.' Three people asked if you were angry."
Akash winced. "I just wanted it to stand out."
"It stood out, all right. It sounds like shouting. And it's one giant paragraph. I couldn't find the time."
"So what do I do?"
"Put the key facts in a short list. Date, time, meeting point, what to bring. Bold just one line, the thing that really matters."
Akash tried: a greeting, then four lines. Sunday, 6 a.m., college gate, and "**Wear proper shoes: the trail is rocky.**"
Bhavna read it. "See? Now it's clear, and you sound like a person."
Two minutes later, replies came in: thumbs up, "got it", "thanks Akash!" Nobody asked if he was angry.

qa.q: Where does the trek group meet?
qa.a: At the college gate.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when Bhavna said three people asked if he was angry?
qa.a: He winced, feeling embarrassed that his capitals read as shouting when he only wanted the message to stand out.

qa.q: What changes made Akash's message clearer?
qa.a: A short list of key facts and bold for only the one line that mattered, instead of all capitals in one long paragraph.

qa.q: How did the club members read the first message?
qa.a: They read the capitals as shouting, and three asked if Akash was angry.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to use lists and a single bold line for clarity, since overused capitals can seem aggressive.

passage: When I became secretary of the college photography club, my first announcement was a disaster. I'm Tejas. I wrote one enormous paragraph about the exhibition, the deadlines, the rules and the prizes, with random words in capitals and six exclamation marks. Sarita, the treasurer, messaged me privately: "Nobody will read this. I couldn't find the deadline." I felt defensive at first. Then I asked five members; four hadn't read past the first line. So I rewrote it. A one-line opening. Then a list: deadline, entry size, where to submit. One line in bold: "Last date: 15 March." I quoted the rules from the old notice instead of retyping them, so nobody would argue about wording. Line breaks between sections. The second version got thirty entries by the first week. Sarita sent me a thumbs-up. I learned that emphasis works best when it's rare.

qa.q: What was the one line in bold?
qa.a: "Last date: 15 March."

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when Sarita said nobody would read it?
qa.a: Tejas felt defensive at first, then realised Sarita was right after asking five members.

qa.q: What made the second announcement work better?
qa.a: A short opening, a list of key facts, one bold line for the deadline, quoted rules and clear line breaks.

qa.q: How did Sarita experience the first announcement?
qa.a: Sarita found it too long and cluttered to read and couldn't even find the deadline.

grounding: Shows a young adult using lists, line breaks, quoting and a single bold line to make a message clear, and seeing how overuse clutters.

passage:
Supervisor's note, logistics internship, week five.
Pankaj is quick and careful, but his emails have been causing friction. Last week he sent the warehouse team a message with every second phrase in bold, three lines in red capitals ("DO NOT SHIP BEFORE CHECKING!!!") and underlines on top. The warehouse head, Imran, called me and asked whether Pankaj was angry with his team. He wasn't; he was worried about a mistake from the previous month. I sat with Pankaj and showed him how the email looked from the other side. He was surprised and a bit embarrassed. We rewrote it together: a polite greeting, three numbered steps, one bold line for the key check, and a quoted line from the shipping policy so it didn't sound like his personal rule. He sent it again with a short apology for the tone. Imran replied, "Clear now, thanks." I'll keep reviewing Pankaj's emails for another two weeks.
— Supervisor, Rekha Iyer

qa.q: How many numbered steps did the rewritten email have?
qa.a: Three numbered steps.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he saw how his email looked to others?
qa.a: He was surprised and a bit embarrassed, since he had only been worried about a repeat mistake, not angry.

qa.q: How did the supervisor help Pankaj fix the email?
qa.a: Rekha Iyer showed him how it read from the other side, then helped him rewrite it with numbered steps, one bold line and a quoted policy line.

qa.q: How did Imran read the first email?
qa.a: He wondered if Pankaj was angry with his team, because of all the bold, capitals and exclamation marks.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that overused bold and capitals seem aggressive, and using structure and one emphasis to be clear.

passage: Last month I posted in our class group about Mridul's surprise birthday: a plan, a time, a shared cost. I'm Sunaina. The message showed "Seen by 23". Replies: zero. For two hours nothing. I kept checking. I felt stupid, like everyone thought my plan was silly, or worse, that they didn't care about me. I almost deleted it. Then Mridul, who wasn't in the group, called me about something else, and I blurted it out. He laughed. "It's exam week! Half of them read everything at the library and forget to reply. And people hate committing to money in a group." That evening, replies trickled in: "sorry, lab all day", "count me in", "can I pay later?" By night eighteen people had said yes. Looking back, I'd read the silence as a feeling about me. It was mostly just people being busy.

qa.q: How many people had said yes by night?
qa.a: Eighteen people.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling during the two hours of silence?
qa.a: Sunaina felt stupid and hurt, worried everyone thought the plan was silly or didn't care.

qa.q: What did Sunaina learn about reading group chat silence?
qa.a: That slow replies usually reflect busyness or hesitation about money, not feelings about the sender.

qa.q: How did Mridul explain the silence?
qa.a: He said it was exam week, people read at the library and forget to reply, and many avoid committing to money in a group.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading group chat silence and read receipts as feelings, when they reflected busyness.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, boys' wing, Tuesday.
Karthik, a first-year, came to my office late last night, upset. He showed me his phone: his floor's group chat. He'd posted a long message asking if anyone wanted to form a study group. Twenty people had seen it; only two had reacted with a thumbs-up, and nobody replied. "They all hate me," he said. "They talk in the group all day, but not to me." I asked him to scroll up. Many messages in that group got no replies either. It was 11 p.m., the night before a test. I suggested the silence was more likely busy people than a judgement about him, but that he could check by asking one or two directly. This morning he told me he'd knocked on Arjun's door, and Arjun said he'd seen the message but was cramming and forgot. They're meeting on Thursday. I'll keep an eye on how Karthik settles in.
— Sudha Menon

qa.q: How many people reacted with a thumbs-up?
qa.a: Only two.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he came to the warden's office?
qa.a: He was upset and lonely, convinced everyone hated him because of the silence.

qa.q: What did Sudha suggest that helped?
qa.a: She pointed out that many messages got no replies and suggested checking directly with one or two people instead of trusting the silence.

qa.q: How did Arjun explain not replying?
qa.a: He had seen the message but was cramming for the test and forgot.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading group chat silence as rejection and learning, by asking directly, that it reflected busyness.

passage:
Saturday night.
Yusuf left me on "read" for two days. Two blue ticks under my long message about the college fest band. I checked about fifty times. I was sure he was annoyed; I'd pushed him hard to join.
Tonight I finally saw him at the chai stall. Before I could say anything, he said, "Sorry man, saw your message on the bus, meant to reply, then Nani was unwell and we were at the hospital all Friday." I felt terrible for building a whole story in my head.
Then I noticed something else. In the band group, Imtiaz replies in two seconds to everything, and Rohit only ever sends a thumbs-up, and it doesn't mean anything about how either of them feels. It's just how they use their phones.
Rule for me: ticks are not feelings.
— Shankar

qa.q: How long did Yusuf leave Shankar on read?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling during the two days?
qa.a: Shankar felt anxious and sure Yusuf was annoyed, checking the phone about fifty times.

qa.q: What rule did Shankar make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: "Ticks are not feelings", because read receipts and slow replies often reflect busy lives, not how people feel.

qa.q: Why hadn't Yusuf replied?
qa.a: His Nani was unwell and he was at the hospital all Friday, so he forgot after reading it on the bus.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading read receipts and slow replies as feelings, and learning they are unreliable evidence.

passage: It was 11 p.m., the night before the final exam, when the class group exploded. Someone had posted that Parveen had leaked the question paper. It wasn't true. Within minutes, forty messages: accusations, jokes, one person calling her a cheat and worse. Parveen's hands were shaking. She typed a furious reply, then stopped. Her friend Yamini called. "Don't reply in the group. Not angry. Not tonight." Parveen deleted her draft. Instead, she took screenshots of every message, especially the abusive one from a boy outside their class. She sent one calm line to the group: "That's false. I'll speak to the class teacher tomorrow." Then she muted it, reported the abusive account, and blocked him. At 11:30 she called her mother, then forwarded the screenshots to the class teacher. The teacher replied before midnight: "Thank you for telling me. I'll deal with this in the morning. Please rest."

qa.q: What time did the class group explode?
qa.a: At 11 p.m., the night before the final exam.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling as the messages poured in?
qa.a: She was upset and furious, her hands shaking, and almost replied in anger.

qa.q: Which steps helped Parveen handle the thread?
qa.a: Not replying angrily, taking screenshots, posting one calm line, muting, reporting and blocking the abuser, and telling her mother and teacher that night.

qa.q: How did the class teacher respond when Parveen forwarded the screenshots?
qa.a: The teacher replied before midnight, thanked her, promised to deal with it in the morning and told her to rest.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing a heated, abusive thread by pausing, not replying in anger, keeping screenshots, blocking and reporting, and getting support.

passage: Nikita posted a video of her kathak practice on her public profile. By evening, most comments were kind, but one account kept posting ugly remarks about her body, then messages to her inbox. She showed Santosh, her classmate, in the Pune college canteen. Her voice was tight. "I want to reply and tell him exactly what he is." Santosh understood the urge. "You can. But he wants a fight. What if we don't give him one?" Together they took screenshots of every comment and message, with dates showing. Nikita reported the account for harassment and blocked it. Then she turned comments to friends-only for a week. "Should I tell someone?" she asked. "Yes, today," Santosh said. They went to the college's women's cell that afternoon. The counsellor there looked through the screenshots and said, "You did exactly right. We'll help you file a cyber complaint if it continues."

qa.q: Where did Nikita show Santosh the comments?
qa.a: In the Pune college canteen.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling about the comments?
qa.a: She was upset and angry, her voice tight, wanting to reply and tell the harasser exactly what he was.

qa.q: What steps did Nikita and Santosh take instead of fighting back?
qa.a: They took dated screenshots, reported and blocked the account, limited comments, and went to the women's cell the same day.

qa.q: How did the counsellor respond at the women's cell?
qa.a: The counsellor reviewed the screenshots, said Nikita had done exactly right, and offered to help file a cyber complaint if it continued.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing online harassment by not replying in anger, saving screenshots, blocking, reporting and seeking support.

passage:
"Your post about the hostel food. You tagged me," Kalyani said, her phone out. "Forty people are now saying I complained to the warden."
"I didn't mean it like that," Avni said. "I just said you'd agree with me."
"I nearly replied under it. In capitals."
"I saw you typing. Then you stopped."
"I stopped because I was too angry. I'd have said something I couldn't take back."
Avni sat down. "Okay. I'm listening."
"I didn't complain to anyone. Now the mess staff think I did. Can you take the tag off and say it was your view?"
"Yes. Doing it now." Avni typed. "Done. I'm sorry. I should've asked before tagging you."
Kalyani let out a breath. "Thanks. Honestly, this was easier face to face."
"Much," Avni said. "The comments were getting nasty."

qa.q: How many people were saying Kalyani complained to the warden?
qa.a: Forty people.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she almost replied in capitals?
qa.a: She was very angry, and worried she would say something she couldn't take back.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do that calmed the conflict?
qa.a: She paused instead of replying in anger and moved the talk face to face, calmly asking Avni to remove the tag.

qa.q: How did Avni respond when Kalyani explained the problem?
qa.a: She listened, removed the tag straight away, apologised and admitted she should have asked first.

grounding: Shows a young adult pausing instead of replying angrily online and moving a heated thread into a private conversation.

subtype: Acting a role versus feeling it [Mismatch]
passage: The power went out at the final dress rehearsal, twenty minutes before the college drama society's show. The hall went black, then phone torches came on. The director shouted, "Keep going! Use the torches!" Sarita, playing a mother whose son had died, stepped into the pool of light. Her voice cracked. Her hands shook as she folded the boy's shirt. Real tears ran down her face. In the front row, her friend Ayesha, who'd come to help with costumes, felt her own throat ache. After the scene, Ayesha hurried backstage. "Sarita, are you okay? Is something wrong at home?" Sarita laughed, wiping her face with a tissue. "I'm fine! I think about the timing of each breath, and I press my tongue hard to the roof of my mouth. The tears just come." Ayesha stared. "It looked so real." "That's the job," Sarita said, and went to fix her make-up.

qa.q: What was Sarita's character doing when her hands shook?
qa.a: Folding the boy's shirt.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling as she watched the scene?
qa.a: She was moved and worried, her throat aching, and she feared Sarita was truly upset about something at home.

qa.q: What does Ayesha learn from Sarita's answer?
qa.a: That visible emotion on stage can be crafted with technique, so a display is not proof of the actor's own state.

qa.q: How did Sarita see her own tears?
qa.a: As part of her craft, produced by timing her breath and a physical trick, not a sign that she was actually sad.

grounding: Shows a young actor crafting a convincing display of grief, and a friend learning not to equate the display with the actor's own feelings.

subtype: Acting a role versus feeling it [Mismatch]
passage: After the college play in Pune, Divyansh walked out to the foyer still in his black villain's coat. He'd spent two hours snarling, threatening and laughing coldly at the hero. His friend Lokesh had brought his mother and younger sister. The sister, about ten, stepped behind her mother when Divyansh came near. Lokesh's mother smiled politely but seemed a little cool. "You were very frightening," she said. Divyansh grinned, then noticed they weren't smiling back. He bent down to the girl and took off the coat. "It's just a costume. I practised the evil laugh in the bathroom mirror for a week. My mother kept knocking to ask if I was choking." The girl giggled. Lokesh's mother laughed properly now. "So you're actually nice?" "I'm told I'm very boring," Divyansh said. "My roommate says I apologise to chairs."

qa.q: How long did Divyansh practise the evil laugh?
qa.a: For a week.

qa.q: What was Lokesh's younger sister feeling when Divyansh came near?
qa.a: She was frightened, stepping behind her mother because he still looked like the villain.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that helped the family relax?
qa.a: He took off the costume and shared funny details about practising the laugh, showing the villain was a crafted role.

qa.q: How did Lokesh's mother see Divyansh at first?
qa.a: She seemed a little cool, as if some of the villain's nastiness might be real, until he joked about himself.

grounding: Shows a young actor playing a villain convincingly without feeling it, and an audience learning not to confuse the display with the actor.

subtype: Acting a role versus feeling it [Mismatch]
passage:
"How did you do that?" Jomon asked, catching Zainab outside the auditorium. "When your character heard about the accident. I actually felt sick."
Zainab laughed. "Good. That was the plan."
"But were you feeling it? Really?"
"Not the way you think. I was counting."
"Counting?"
"Three beats of stillness, then the breath in, then I let my knees go. The director made me do it forty times."
"So you weren't sad at all?"
"Some nights a bit, if I think of my grandfather. Tonight I was mostly worried about my shoe coming off."
Jomon shook his head. "I was ready to hug you afterwards."
"You can hug me anyway. But don't worry about me. The character's the one who's heartbroken."
"That's a bit scary. How do I know when anyone's real?"
Zainab shrugged. "On stage you don't. Off stage, you ask."

qa.q: How many times did the director make Zainab practise the moment?
qa.a: Forty times.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling during tonight's performance?
qa.a: She was mostly focused and slightly worried about her shoe coming off, not heartbroken like her character.

qa.q: What does Zainab's advice suggest about reading emotion?
qa.a: That on stage a display can be crafted, so off stage it is better to ask how someone really feels than to assume.

qa.q: How did Jomon experience the scene?
qa.a: He was so moved that he felt sick and was ready to hug Zainab, believing the grief was real.

grounding: Shows a young actor crafting visible grief with technique and a friend learning not to equate display with the actor's own state.

subtype: Cultural performance and shared ritual arts [Expressing]
passage:
Dear Madhuri,
You asked why I spent every evening for a month practising garba for the college fest when I'm "not even that religious". I've been thinking about how to explain.
At home in Vadodara, Navratri isn't a show. It's nine nights of my whole street dancing in circles around the goddess's lamp, Ba in the middle clapping, my cousins teaching the little ones the steps. When I dance, I'm not just doing footwork. I'm thanking the goddess the way Ba does, and I'm back in that street with my family, even here in Bengaluru.
At the fest someone called it "that cute dandiya thing". I didn't mind the word cute. But it isn't only a dance to me.
Come to our practice on Thursday? I'll teach you the three-clap step, and you can ask anything.
Damini

qa.q: Where does Damini's family celebrate Navratri?
qa.a: In Vadodara, on their street.

qa.q: What does Damini feel when dancing garba?
qa.a: Damini feels devoted and connected to family, as if back on the street at home while thanking the goddess.

qa.q: What does Damini invite Madhuri to do, and why is it a good way to learn?
qa.a: To come to practice and ask anything, which lets Madhuri learn the context before judging the dance.

qa.q: How did the person at the fest seem to see the garba?
qa.a: They saw it as a cute dance, not knowing the devotion and family meaning behind it for Damini.

grounding: Shows a young adult performing garba as an expression of devotion and belonging, and inviting others to ask about its context.

subtype: Cultural performance and shared ritual arts [Expressing]
passage: Ojas, you asked me on your channel what kathak means to me. I'm Anjali, and I've danced it since I was seven. At our college fest last year, I performed a piece about Radha waiting for Krishna. Afterwards a boy from my class said, "Nice spinning. Very Bollywood." I wanted to scream. But I also realised he'd never seen kathak before. So I found him later and asked, "Want to know what the spins were?" He shrugged, then said yes. I explained that the chakkars and footwork are rhythm conversations with the tabla, and every hand gesture in that piece told part of the story. That the waiting was devotion, for me, not just romance. He was quiet for a bit and then asked, "So when your eyes looked left, that was her looking for him?" I said yes. He came to our next performance and sat in the front row.

qa.q: What was Anjali's piece about?
qa.a: Radha waiting for Krishna.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when the boy called it "Very Bollywood"?
qa.a: Anjali felt frustrated and hurt, wanting to scream, since kathak means so much more to Anjali.

qa.q: What did Anjali do instead of snapping back?
qa.a: Anjali offered to explain the dance's meaning, rhythm and gestures, giving him context instead of judging him.

qa.q: How did the boy's view of the kathak change?
qa.a: After learning its meaning, he understood details like the eye movements and came to the next performance in the front row.

grounding: Shows a young adult performing kathak as devotion and tradition, and helping a learner understand context before judging.

subtype: Cultural performance and shared ritual arts [Expressing]
passage: I'm Neelam, and I'd never seen Bihu before Bhupen and his friends performed it at our college fest in Pune. The dhol started, the pepa horn wailed, and Bhupen and five others in cream and red gamosas leapt onto the stage. Their movements were fast, bouncy, full of smiles. I thought it was a party dance. Then, during the slower part, Bhupen's face changed; his eyes went soft, and he looked almost homesick. Afterwards, I asked him about it instead of guessing. He said Rongali Bihu is the spring and harvest festival back home in Assam, and for him it's about the fields, his grandparents, and new beginnings. "The fast part is joy. The slow part, for me, is missing home." I don't know if everyone in the group felt that. But I'm glad I asked, because I'd have written it off as just a happy dance.

qa.q: What colours were the gamosas?
qa.a: Cream and red.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling during the slower part of the dance?
qa.a: He seemed homesick, missing home and his grandparents, even though the fast part expressed joy.

qa.q: What did Neelam do that others could learn from?
qa.a: Neelam asked Bhupen about the dance's meaning instead of guessing, which revealed the context.

qa.q: How did Neelam first see the Bihu dance?
qa.a: As a party dance, fast and happy, before learning it also carried harvest, family and homesickness.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult performing Bihu to express pride and longing, and the value of asking about context.

passage:
"So? What did you think?" Sudha asked, her voice unsteady. Her short film had just finished playing to the class.
Pradeep hesitated. "It was so sad. Your grandmother alone on that train, the empty house at the end. I nearly cried."
"Sad?" Sudha frowned. "The empty house was meant to be hopeful. She's starting over."
"Oh. The music was so slow, though. And the grey colours."
"I chose grey because that's how I remember her old village. The slow music was her favourite song."
"Well, to me it felt like loss. Maybe because my Dadi died last year."
Sudha was quiet. "Then maybe it's both."
"Is that bad?"
"No." She smiled a little. "I guess once it's out there, people bring their own stories. I'll add one shot of her smiling in the new house, though. Just so the hope shows."

qa.q: Why did Sudha choose grey colours for the film?
qa.a: Because that's how she remembers her grandmother's old village.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when Pradeep called the film sad?
qa.a: She was surprised and a little disappointed, since she had meant the ending to be hopeful.

qa.q: What did Sudha decide to do, and why is it reasonable?
qa.a: Add a shot of her grandmother smiling in the new house to make the hope clearer, while accepting that viewers bring their own stories.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep read the film as sad?
qa.a: The slow music and grey colours, together with his own grief for his Dadi, shaped his reading.

grounding: Shows a young filmmaker communicating a viewpoint and learning that audiences read work through their own experience.

passage: For my final-year design project, I made a poster about water in our city: a cracked earthen pot with a single tap dripping above it. I'm Hafsa. To me, it was about my Ammi carrying water from the tanker every summer in our lane in Hyderabad, and about patience. When it went up in the corridor, my classmate Suraj said it was "angry", a protest against the government. A professor said it was "about climate change". A cleaner stopped in front of it for a long time and told me it reminded her of her village. At first I felt a bit annoyed; none of them saw my Ammi. Then I realised nobody could, unless I told them. They were bringing their own lives to it. I added a small line of text at the bottom, "For Ammi, who waited", and let the rest stay open.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's poster show?
qa.a: A cracked earthen pot with a single tap dripping above it.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when others read the poster differently?
qa.a: Hafsa felt a bit annoyed at first, then accepting, realising viewers bring their own lives to the work.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do to share her intent without closing other readings?
qa.a: Hafsa added a small dedication, "For Ammi, who waited", and let the rest of the poster stay open.

qa.q: How did the cleaner experience the poster?
qa.a: It reminded her of her village, so she stopped in front of it for a long time.

grounding: Shows a young designer communicating a personal meaning to strangers and learning that intent and reception can differ.

passage:
Studio tutor's note, architecture final jury, Friday.
Chetan presented his design for a bus shelter on the old market road. He had built it with low, curved concrete walls and deep shade, and explained that it was meant to feel like his grandmother's verandah in Bhuj: a place to rest and talk. One juror, Mr Ramesh, a visiting architect, read it very differently. "Those low walls feel like a bunker. Defensive. Is this about fear?" Chetan looked thrown. I watched him take a breath. Then he asked, "Which part feels defensive to you?" Mr Ramesh pointed to the narrow openings. Chetan admitted he hadn't thought about how they looked from the road. He sketched wider openings on the spot. Mr Ramesh nodded. "Now it's a verandah." Later Chetan told me he was glad the reading was different; it showed him something he couldn't see.
— Tutor, Anita Rao

qa.q: Where did Chetan design the bus shelter?
qa.a: On the old market road.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when Mr Ramesh called the shelter a bunker?
qa.a: He looked thrown, probably surprised and a little hurt, since he meant it to feel like his grandmother's verandah.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that turned the criticism into learning?
qa.a: He asked which part felt defensive and then sketched wider openings on the spot.

qa.q: How did Mr Ramesh read the design at first?
qa.a: As defensive and bunker-like, because the low walls and narrow openings looked closed from the road.

grounding: Shows a young architect communicating a feeling through design and learning that viewers read the work through their own experience.

passage: At the college gallery's student show, Payal and I stood in front of a huge dark canvas: black, deep blue, one thin red line. I'm Ayesha. I said confidently, "Whoever painted this was really depressed." Payal raised her eyebrows. "Maybe." That evening the painter, a third-year named Rizwan, gave a short talk. He said he'd been studying an old Japanese ink style that uses mostly dark tones, and the red line was a trick he'd learned to lead the eye. He said he'd painted it during the happiest month of his year, after his sister's wedding. I felt silly. I'd read his whole mind from the colours. Payal whispered, "You'd have said the same about half the paintings in the museum." Since then, when I look at art, I try to say, "This makes me feel…", not "the artist felt…".

qa.q: What was the painting's one bright element?
qa.a: One thin red line.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel after hearing Rizwan's talk?
qa.a: Ayesha felt silly and a bit embarrassed for assuming the painter was depressed from the colours.

qa.q: What habit did Ayesha adopt, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Saying "This makes me feel…" instead of "the artist felt…", because a maker's mood can't be safely read from the work alone.

qa.q: How did Rizwan explain the dark painting?
qa.a: He said it came from studying an old ink style and a technique to lead the eye, and he painted it during a happy month.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that art reflects craft and tradition, so the maker's mood can't be inferred from the work alone.

passage:
Film studies teacher's note, Tuesday seminar.
Today we watched a short black-and-white film about an old man feeding pigeons. Anjali, in the discussion, said firmly, "The director must be lonely. You can feel it." Several students nodded. I asked Darshan, who had read the director's interview for homework, to share what he'd found. The director had made the film as a comedy about his own father, who is surrounded by family and loves pigeons, and chose black and white because of a festival rule. Anjali looked embarrassed, then curious. She asked, "So the loneliness is just in me?" I said her reading was valid as her own response, but that we can't safely read the director's mood from the screen. Craft, tradition and audience all shape a film. I've asked the class to write two paragraphs next week: one on what the film made them feel, one on what they know of how it was made.
— Mr Kurian

Thursday night.
Went to the screening of Kashish's friend's short film at the film club. The film was so bleak: rain, an empty bus stop, a girl waiting for someone who never came. I left thinking the director must be heartbroken. I even asked Kashish, very seriously, if her friend was okay.
Kashish laughed so hard. "Tara? She's the most cheerful person I know. She made it for an assignment on 'waiting'. The rain was a sprinkler, and she had to reshoot because she kept giggling."
I felt a bit foolish. I'd built a whole sad story about a person from twelve minutes of film.
But the film did make me feel something real. That part's mine, I think. The director's feelings are hers, and I don't know them.
— Bhupen

subtype: Sculpture as expression of inner states [Expressing]
passage: Ojas, you asked why I keep that crooked clay figure on my desk. Let your Zubin mama tell you. When I was twenty, my father died suddenly, a week before my exams. I didn't cry. I couldn't talk to anyone. My sister thought I didn't care. At the art college studio, I took a lump of clay and pressed and twisted it for three nights, not planning anything. It became a man bent over, hands pressed to his chest. My teacher, Mrs Irani, looked at it and said, "It's very strong. It looks like pride." I nearly laughed. For me it was all the grief I couldn't say. But she wasn't wrong either. My father was a proud man. Later my sister saw it and cried, and then I cried, finally, with her. That lump said what my mouth couldn't. And each of us saw our own father in it.

qa.q: How many nights did young Zubin work on the clay?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: What was young Zubin feeling while shaping the clay?
qa.a: He was grieving deeply, unable to cry or talk, and the clay let that grief out.

qa.q: What turning point came from the sculpture?
qa.a: His sister saw it and cried, and then Zubin finally cried with her, sharing the grief he couldn't speak.

qa.q: How did Mrs Irani read the sculpture?
qa.a: She saw it as strong and full of pride, a reading different from Zubin's intent but still true to his father.

grounding: Shows a young adult expressing grief through a clay sculpture, where the maker's intent and a viewer's reading differ and both are valid.

subtype: Sculpture as expression of inner states [Expressing]
passage: The exhibition opened at ten the next morning, and the college kiln had broken, so Aditi's clay piece was ruined. With twelve hours left, she switched to wood. She carved two hands clasped so tightly that the knuckles stood out, working by lamp in the hostel common room. Her hands ached. She was thinking of her parents' fights, the way her mother held her own hands in her lap to stop them shaking. She didn't tell anyone. At the opening, her friend Kiran stood before it. "It's about pride, isn't it? Like holding on to something you've won." Aditi almost corrected her. Then she said, "What makes you say pride?" "The strength in it. They won't let go." Aditi nodded slowly. "For me it's tension. Holding on so you don't break." Kiran looked again. "I can see that too, now. Both are in there."

qa.q: When did the exhibition open?
qa.a: At ten the next morning.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling as she carved the hands?
qa.a: She was tense and troubled, thinking of her parents' fights and her mother holding her hands to stop them shaking.

qa.q: How did Aditi respond to Kiran's different reading?
qa.a: She asked what made Kiran see pride, then shared her own meaning, so both readings could sit together.

qa.q: How did Kiran first read the sculpture?
qa.a: As pride and holding on to something won, because of the strength in the clasped hands.

grounding: Shows a young adult expressing tension through a sculpture under time pressure, and maker's intent and viewer's reading differing but both valid.

subtype: Sculpture as expression of inner states [Expressing]
passage: In her small room in a Kolkata mess, Rekha had spent a month building a sculpture from old glass bangles: dozens of them, red and green, melted and fused into a twisted column. The bangles were her grandmother's; after Thakuma's death, the family had given them to Rekha. At the college exhibition, her classmate Usha stood in front of it for a long time. "It's so festive," Usha said. "Like a wedding." Rekha's throat tightened. "They were my grandmother's. She died in March." Usha's face fell. "Oh, Rekha. I'm sorry. I didn't know." Rekha shook her head. "No, don't be sorry. She wore them at every wedding in the family. Maybe that's in there too." Usha looked again, quieter. "It's grief and celebration, then." Rekha smiled for the first time that evening. "Yes. That's exactly what she was."

qa.q: What was Rekha's sculpture made from?
qa.a: Old glass bangles, red and green, melted and fused into a twisted column.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when Usha called the sculpture festive?
qa.a: Her throat tightened with grief, because the bangles were her grandmother's and she had died in March.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that allowed both readings to stand?
qa.a: She shared the story of the bangles but welcomed Usha's reading, since her grandmother wore them at every wedding.

qa.q: How did Usha's view of the sculpture change?
qa.a: She first saw it as festive like a wedding, then, after hearing Rekha, as grief and celebration together.

grounding: Shows a young adult expressing grief and pride through a found-object sculpture, with maker's and viewer's readings both valid.

passage:
Tuesday.
Finally decided about the tattoo. I've wanted Nana's handwriting on my forearm since he died, the words from his last letter: "Stay kind." Manoj came with me to the studio to look at designs.
The artist asked good questions. "How will you feel about it at forty? Does your job have rules?" I hadn't thought about the bank internship. Some branches expect sleeves down with customers. Manoj said his cousin had to wear full sleeves every day in summer because of his tattoo.
So I changed the plan a little. Not the forearm; the upper arm, where a short sleeve still covers it. Smaller. Same words, same handwriting.
I booked for next month, not today. If I still want it in four weeks, I'll know. I think I will. It feels like carrying him with me.
— Raghav

passage: In the village of Namchi, Dolma had decided on a tattoo: a small snow mountain behind her ear, for the hills she'd grown up in and was leaving for college in Delhi. Her brother Sumit frowned when she told him at the tea stall. "Behind the ear? What about your police recruitment exam next year? Some forces have rules about tattoos." Dolma paused. She hadn't thought of that. "You don't know that for sure." "No. So check." That evening she looked up the recruitment notice on the district office board, and found that tattoos were allowed only in some places on the body. Behind the ear wasn't one of them. Dolma was disappointed. But she didn't give up. She chose the inside of her forearm, where the notice allowed small designs. "It's the same mountain," she told Sumit. "Just a different spot." He grinned. "And still my sister."

"Suit or kurta?" Saurabh held up both on hangers.

passage: At my first campus placement interview, I wore my uncle's borrowed suit, a size too big, and a tie I'd learned to knot from a video that morning. I'm Nitin. I felt like an actor. In the waiting room, I looked around and judged everyone. The boy in the shiny shoes looked like a topper. Payal, in a simple cotton kurta and flat sandals, looked, I thought, unprepared. I even felt a bit sorry for her. Then, in the group discussion, Payal was the best person in the room. Calm, sharp, she summed up everyone's points and fixed an error the shiny-shoes boy made. She got the offer; I didn't. On the bus home, I kept thinking about how quickly I'd sorted people by their clothes. Dressing well helped me feel serious. But it told me nothing about who could actually do the job.

qa.q: What did Payal wear to the interview?
qa.a: A simple cotton kurta and flat sandals.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Nitin felt humbled and a bit ashamed of how quickly clothes had been used to judge people.

qa.q: What lesson did Nitin take from the day?
qa.a: That dressing well can help one feel serious, but clothing tells little about someone's ability.

qa.q: How might Payal have experienced others' first impressions of her?
qa.a: She may have been underestimated at first because of her simple clothes, until her performance in the discussion changed that.

grounding: Shows a young adult choosing formal clothing for an interview and learning that first impressions from dress are unreliable measures of ability.
